hero.headline: Vero Beach's MusicWorks launches fourteenth concert season to expand cultural tourism
hero.body:
MusicWorks in Vero Beach has launched its fourteenth concert season as part of a broader effort to expand cultural tourism across multiple states. The organization is targeting audiences in California, Texas, New York, Tennessee, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, Arizona, Michigan and Massachusetts as part of its multi-state travel initiative. This expanded marketing approach aims to draw visitors from across the country to Indian River County specifically for the concert programming.

The new season represents a strategic shift toward positioning Vero Beach as a cultural destination that competes with arts programming in larger metropolitan areas across the nation. By directing promotional efforts toward ten target states, MusicWorks seeks to establish Indian River County as a destination for live performance experiences. The initiative aligns with growing trends in cultural tourism that focus on attracting out-of-state visitors to smaller Florida markets beyond the state's traditional beach and theme park attractions.

MusicWorks has established itself as a cornerstone of the local arts community over its thirteen previous seasons of operation. The organization has built its reputation through consistent concert programming and community engagement in Vero Beach. As cultural tourism initiatives increasingly recognize the value of arts and entertainment in driving regional visitation, MusicWorks has positioned itself to capitalize on this growing interest in destination-based cultural experiences.

The fourteenth season launch represents continued investment in Vero Beach's cultural infrastructure alongside its established coastal attractions. Concert details and scheduling for the new season are being actively promoted to potential audiences across the identified target markets. By focusing on multi-state travel inspiration, MusicWorks demonstrates confidence in its programming's appeal to visitors beyond Florida's borders. The organization's approach reflects a recognition that cultural events can serve as compelling reasons for travelers to choose specific destinations, helping smaller markets like Vero Beach compete for tourism dollars in an increasingly competitive landscape.

cards.headline: Woman, 78, killed after SUV rolls backward in Port St. Lucie driveway
cards.teaser: A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St.
cards.body: A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The incident happened at approximately 10:47 a.m. A 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV was parked in a residential driveway when the woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door. The SUV began rolling backward, and the open door struck her, knocking her to the ground. Her adult son, 59, was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The woman was rushed to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation.

cards.headline: DeSantis vetoes inmate truck driver training and naturopathic medicine board
cards.teaser: Gov.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis vetoed two bills Friday night that had passed unanimously in both chambers. The first veto rejected HB 325, which would have extended commercial driver's license training to nonviolent inmates with two years or less remaining on their sentences. DeSantis said lawmakers overlooked unintended consequences and called the program unnecessarily burdensome to the Department of Corrections, warning that training inmates to drive creates significant public safety concerns. Legislators argued the measure would add no new costs or strain to the prison system. According to the House bill analysis, the legislation responded to a national shortage of about 80,000 commercial truck drivers, with the industry facing replacement of some 1.2 million retiring drivers over the coming decade. The truck driver shortage has put more foreign-born drivers behind the wheel, sometimes with deadly results. Harjinder Singh, trained and licensed outside Florida, is accused of making an illegal U-turn on the Florida Turnpike that killed three people. Singh faces triple vehicular homicide charges and drew national coverage after he was allowed to leave the state. Lt. Gov. Jay Collins flew to California to extradite him, a task State Troopers would ordinarily handle.

DeSantis also vetoed SB 688, legislation that would have created a Board of Naturopathic Medicine within the Department of Health to set guidelines for practitioners. DeSantis previously vetoed bills to track e-bike and scooter crashes and to make it easier for high school students to volunteer as poll workers. More vetoes are coming, specifically line items in the budget, which DeSantis is expected to sign Monday ahead of the new fiscal year July 1.

cards.headline: Jupiter firefighters deploy to Venezuela earthquake rescue mission with 24 hours notice
cards.body:
Two firefighters from Jupiter Fire Rescue have joined an 80-member FEMA Urban Search and Rescue Task Force heading to Venezuela to support earthquake relief operations. The deployment was activated Sunday with less than 24 hours notice, and the team expects to remain in the affected region for at least two weeks. The mission also includes first responders from Delray Beach and Palm Beach County fire departments.

The rescue operation concentrates on locating and extracting people from collapsed structures, including both large buildings and residential homes. The task force transported specialized equipment designed for heavy-duty rescue work, including tools for breaking through debris, cutting through obstacles, breaching walls, and stabilizing unstable structures. Team members also brought technical rope rescue equipment to handle complex vertical rescue scenarios in damaged buildings.

Stephen Shaw, deputy fire chief of operations for Jupiter Fire Rescue, emphasized that the rapid deployment demonstrates the department's core mission. "This right here represents one of these situations where they need help, people need help and for us at Jupiter Fire Rescue, if someone needs help we go," Shaw said. The decision to send personnel reflects the fire rescue service's commitment to assisting communities in crisis, regardless of location or timeline.

Beyond the immediate humanitarian impact, Shaw noted that the experience will benefit Jupiter Fire Rescue when the team returns home. The real-world training and skills practiced during the rescue mission will strengthen the department's capabilities. "And when they come back the learning that has taken place and the skills that they have been practicing is only going to benefit us internally as we continue to grow our fire department," Shaw explained. The deployment provides valuable professional development for the firefighters involved while contributing to Venezuela's earthquake recovery efforts.

cards.headline: Florida public-sector unions win recertification votes despite state restrictions
cards.teaser: AFSCME Florida continues to post lopsided recertification victories across the state three years after Florida enacted sweeping restrictions on public-sector unions, with recent wins in Jacksonville, Polk County, Miami Gardens, DeFuniak Springs and Naples.
cards.body:
Florida's largest public-sector union has continued posting overwhelming victories in recertification elections across the state, three years after the governor pushed through sweeping restrictions on government worker organizing. Workers in Jacksonville, Polk County, Miami Gardens, DeFuniak Springs and Naples all voted overwhelmingly in recent weeks to retain union representation through AFSCME, according to union officials. The results demonstrate that despite significant initial challenges, AFSCME Florida has adapted to the regulatory changes and rebuilt its membership. Jacksonville city employees voted more than 98% in favor of recertification this week, continuing a successful year for the union. AFSCME Florida reported winning 30 of 32 recertification elections in 2025, with several victories coming from bargaining units that had initially lost certification under the state's 2023 restrictions.

The 2023 law, sponsored by Republican Senator Blaise Ingoglia and championed by Gov. Ron DeSantis, dramatically raised the bar for union organizing in Florida. The measure increased membership requirements from 50% to 60% of a bargaining unit and eliminated automatic dues deductions from employee paychecks. The impact was immediate and severe. By May 2025, more than 100 unions had been decertified across Florida, with roughly 69,000 workers losing representation. AFSCME Local 1279 in Jacksonville was among those initially decertified in February 2024. However, the union recovered by re-registering hundreds of members, establishing a new dues payment system and holding extensive member meetings. In September, Local 1279 secured a new contract with Jacksonville by a 99% vote.

Arthur Finley, president of AFSCME Local 1279, called the 2023 law "massively disruptive legislation" that gave unions insufficient time to adjust. Despite the setback, Finley emphasized that union members remained committed to organizing. "We lost our union at the start, but working with the council and other AFSCME locals in the area, we were able to get on track and win it back," Finley said. The union's recent victories came despite additional restrictions taking effect July 1 through another measure that requires at least 50% of bargaining unit members to vote in certification elections and mandates recertification if dues-paying members fall below 60%.

DeSantis defended the new restrictions as targeting "partisan teacher unions" that lack genuine educator support. However, the Florida Education Association, representing approximately 120,000 members, disputed this characterization and pointed to Florida's poor rankings in teacher compensation and per-student funding. The Florida AFL-CIO countered claims of partisan union organizing, noting that more than 30% of Florida union members identify as Republican. Despite these ongoing legal obstacles, AFSCME's recertification margins, which mostly exceeded 90%, suggest sustained worker support for union representation.

cards.headline: Vero Beach group collects supplies for Venezuela earthquake victims through Saturday
cards.teaser: Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive to collect essential supplies for communities devastated by a massive earthqu.
cards.body:
Latinas Nexus Network in Vero Beach is hosting a Venezuela Earthquake Relief Drive to collect essential supplies for communities devastated by a 7.5 magnitude earthquake in the South American country. Founders Lourana Navarro and Juliana Marino, along with Heidi Ramirez, are organizing the effort in partnership with Global Empowerment Mission to ship collected supplies directly to Venezuela. Donations are being accepted through Saturday, June 27, 2026, from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. at 684 Old Dixie Hwy, Vero Beach. Navarro, who was born in Venezuela and now lives in Vero Beach, said her family in Caracas is safe, but surrounding communities have lost everything. She said the earthquake caused devastation that will take decades to recover from and that the most critical needs right now are food and places to sleep and bathe.

The organizers are collecting powder Gatorade, non-perishable food, baby formula and baby food, diapers in all sizes, baby wipes, feminine hygiene products, soap, shampoo, toothbrushes and toothpaste, rain boots, toilet paper, blankets, sleeping bags, flashlights and batteries, heavy duty garbage bags, first aid kits, bandages and gauze, hand sanitizer, cleaning supplies, face masks, nitrile medical gloves, and plastic bins with lids. The drive is open to everyone, not just the local Hispanic community. Marino said hundreds of thousands of people are in need right now. The organization says 100% of donated supplies will be directed through verified humanitarian relief efforts. To reach the organizers, contact Navarro at (954) 205-0700, Marino at (772) 913-0805, or Ramirez at (772) 213-2747.

The Vero Beach organization is positioning Florida alongside California, Texas, New York, Tennessee, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, Arizona, Michigan and Massachusetts as it begins its new season. The concert series is designed to expand cultural tourism and inspire multi-state travel.

MusicWorks is beginning its fourteenth season of concerts in Vero Beach. The organization is working to bring visitors from across the country to the area for musical performances.

hero.headline: Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce featured in America 250 Road Trip
hero.teaser: The Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday.
hero.body:
The Florida Highwaymen Museum in Fort Pierce is a featured stop on the America 250 Road Trip celebrating the nation's 250th birthday. The city announced the designation on its Facebook page this week.

The museum at 1234 Avenue D opened this year and celebrates 26 Black artists who began painting in the 1950s. The artists created bold, colorful landscapes of Florida's untouched beauty and sold them along the roadside when segregation kept them out of traditional galleries. The museum is the nation's only one with exhibitions that include paintings from each of the 26 renowned Highwaymen artists.

During summer hours from June 16 through July 31, the museum operates Saturday and Sunday from noon to 4 p.m. The museum will be closed in August and reopen in September, featuring a new exhibit.

Fall and spring hours from September 1 through June 15 will be expanded. The museum stands as a tribute to one of America's most iconic art movements, preserving the legacy of artists whose work captured Florida's natural beauty during an era of racial segregation.

cards.headline: West Boca Raton homeowner battles delays over My Safe Florida Home grant
cards.teaser: Anne Bendel completed $8,000 in home improvements but says My Safe Florida Home grant representatives keep requesting additional paperwork despite telling her in May that her application status was complete.
cards.body:
West Boca Raton resident Anne Bendel says her efforts to receive a My Safe Florida Home grant keep facing new hurdles despite completing the required work. Bendel paid $8,000 out of pocket for home improvements and submitted all required paperwork. My Safe Florida Home contacted her in May and told her application status was complete. A week later, representatives with My Safe Florida Home asked for more documentation, including a permit of completion for a large impact window. She provided it but then faced questions about dates. Her application is now back under review, and her hopes for grant money toward the $8,000 she paid are uncertain.

"I did the work, I had it completed, I got the permits, I had the insurance they asked for. Everything is done, but it seems like when everything is done they find some other little task to send you," Bendel said. The My Safe Florida Home program has helped thousands of homeowners across the state with grants of up to $10,000 to fortify homes against storms and earn insurance discounts. WPTV has contacted the Florida Department of Financial Services in Tallahassee about Bendel's case and the status of her grant.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. after Everglades facility closure
cards.teaser: Immigration attorney Richard Hujber says former Alligator Alcatraz detainees have been sent to facilities in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico and as far as Tacoma, Washington, creating challenges for families and legal cases.
cards.body:
Following the closure of the Alligator Alcatraz detention facility in the Florida Everglades, detainees have been transferred to facilities across the country, including Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and Tacoma, Washington. According to immigration attorney Richard Hujber, this geographic dispersal creates significant legal obstacles for those fighting immigration cases. Hujber explained that "there's different laws in different circuit courts in different parts of the country," and some circuits have rejected bond requests entirely. This variation means a detainee's chances of release depend largely on their transfer location. Without access to bond, many face an impossible choice: continue fighting for residency or asylum with minimal prospects, or self-deport. Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that approximately 21,000 people have been deported from Alligator Alcatraz since it opened nearly a year ago.

Some detainees experienced relief before closure. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before the facility shut down and received an order of supervision, allowing him to work, drive, and remain in the U.S. Hernandez described the emotional toll of detention, saying her family "lived every day wondering if our family is safe." Immigration attorney Hujber noted that families often want to continue fighting, but the decision ultimately rests with the detained individuals themselves. The Baker County facility in North Florida remains operational, but for former Alligator Alcatraz detainees now scattered across the country, the future remains filled with uncertainty.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League issues hurricane pet safety guidance
cards.teaser: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create disaster plans for their pets as hurricane season continues through November.
cards.body:
Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League, told WPTV the safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners. The shelter's expert team recommends microchipping pets, ensuring they wear collars with current identification, and maintaining updated microchip registrations with correct contact information.

Peggy Adams recommends introducing pets to a designated safe room ahead of time, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conducting practice runs so the hurricane is not their first time there. Pet owners should prepare an emergency kit with a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. The organization also advises keeping a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an accessible place and maintaining recent photos of pets, ideally with their owner, to help with identification if separated. Florida's hurricane season runs June through November.

cards.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund has achieved a record-breaking milestone in 2026, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded a record $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, according to President Tim Snow. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. The program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

The fund's services extend beyond financial assistance, Vice President of Development Jay Brandt said. Scholars receive mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate planning to attend Georgetown University, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, provides professional, formal, and casual wear to help scholars prepare for interviews, internships, and campus life. The boutique accepts donations of new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories.

cards.headline: Florida sees 200% jump in fatal road rage crashes, second-highest increase in nation
cards.teaser: Fatal crashes involving road rage in Florida jumped from 12 in 2023 to 36 in 2024, a 200% increase that pushed the state into the second most dangerous in the nation for angry confrontations on highways.
cards.body:
A new study by Grigor Law Injury Car Accident Lawyers found that Florida recorded the nation's second-largest year-over-year increase in fatal road rage crashes. The study examined data from the Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), operated by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, between 2020 and 2024. Fatal crashes involving road rage jumped from 12 in 2023 to 36 in 2024, representing a 200% increase. Only Wyoming topped Florida in increases in fatal road rage incidents, with a 300% jump from one fatal anger-related accident in 2023 to four in 2024. Texas ranked third with an 83.33% increase in road rage fatalities, rising from six in 2023 to 11 in 2024.

Other states in the top 10 for fatal road rage incidents showed varying increases. Alabama came in seventh with a 27.03% jump, with figures increasing from 74 to 94 fatalities. Colorado came in eighth with an 8.33% increase but recorded substantially higher raw numbers than most states, jumping from 120 incidents in 2023 to 130 in 2024. South Carolina also recorded high numbers of road rage fatalities with a 1.82% increase between 2023 and 2024, rising from 55 crashes to 56. The study concluded that Floridians have serious issues controlling their tempers while traveling in autos.

cards.headline: DeSantis praises World Cup visitors while his own rhetoric fuels negative views of America
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis praised the World Cup for giving visiting fans a chance to see America directly, calling it a good country. But his own political brand is built substantially on the premise that a vast, organized internal enemy is destroying the nation.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis praised World Cup visitors for discovering that America is a good country with generous people, despite acknowledging problems and work ahead. However, his political brand, which twice got him elected and made him one of the nation's most influential governors, is built substantially on the premise that vast organized internal enemies are destroying the country. DeSantis has labeled teachers and school administrators who discussed gender identity in classrooms as "groomers" and called corporate executives supporting diversity programs carriers of the "woke mind virus." He described California as "a civilization in decay leading an attack on the American family." This rhetoric portrays powerful forces within America as fundamentally opposed to everything good about it, contradicting his message to World Cup attendees.

The World Cup has created what American political culture cannot seem to produce intentionally: a setting where people from Scotland, Iran, Brazil, Morocco, and Australia interact with actual Americans and discover the caricature is wrong. Fans arrived with whatever impressions their politics and media provided but found something different. DeSantis noted they are "acknowledging that this is a good country." The disconnect raises a fundamental question: when will the people who govern America start acting like they believe the same thing?

cards.headline: Largo reads Pride Month proclamation, launches open-container entertainment district
cards.teaser: Largo Mayor Woody Brown opened the June 2 Commission meeting by reading a Pride Month proclamation after dozens of residents showed up to object when word got out the city had planned to drop it from the agenda entirely.
cards.body:
Largo Mayor Woody Brown read a Pride Month proclamation at the June 2 Commission meeting after the city had initially planned to remove it from the agenda. Dozens of residents attended to object to the removal, many arriving directly from the ribbon-cutting for Horizon West Bay, the $85 million mixed-use development anchored by the city's new City Hall. The same Commission recently passed an ordinance creating a new open-container entertainment district in the blocks surrounding that building, a program called Sip and Stroll that lets patrons walk freely through designated downtown zones with drinks purchased from approved local businesses.

The city faced significant pressure regarding the proclamation. In a June 1 online chat with residents, Brown explained that new legislation barring local governments from spending on diversity, equity and inclusion-related events and initiatives doesn't technically take effect until January, but with the budget still unsigned, the Governor could cut off funding streams Largo depends on, including dollars for stormwater infrastructure. Commissioner Michael Smith, who is gay, pushed back against the near-removal, describing it as a slap in the face and speaking about spending 28 years in the closet. Abner Morales, who owns Wepaa Puerto Rican Restaurant nearby, said the development is awesome because his restaurant has 16 employees and he wants to keep running the business.

cards.headline: Orlando magician Drew Thomas performs residency at Grande Lakes after consulting on Epic Universe
cards.teaser: Drew Thomas, who appeared as a finalist on America's Got Talent Season 4, has lived in Orlando for about a decade and now performs The Magic Show in a residency at Grande Lakes Orlando, home to Ritz-Carlton and JW Marriott hotels.
cards.body:
Orlando magician Drew Thomas has been tapped to consult on Epic Universe, Universal's new theme park that includes a Harry Potter expansion. During the blue sky creative process, Thomas worked on everything from character activities in the park to magical elements in shows, window effects, and how the wands function. This builds on his long history with Universal, including co-creating Jack's Carnival of Wonders, which debuted at Halloween Horror Nights in 2007 and was later revived in 2015. Thomas now performs The Magic Show in a residency at Grande Lakes Orlando, home to the Ritz-Carlton and JW Marriott hotels, with shows scheduled throughout the summer and Halloween and Christmas-themed performances coming later this year.

Thomas' career began at age 16 when he broke his leg skateboarding and decided to pursue magic seriously. His first gig was a kid's birthday party where he performed balloon tricks and magic while wearing a full leg cast, earning $150. At 17, he was hired at a Midwestern chain restaurant to dress as a clown and perform magic table to table. These early experiences helped the naturally shy Thomas learn to think on his feet and deliver quick comebacks. At 40, Thomas performed before America's Got Talent Season 4 judges Simon Cowell, David Hasselhoff, Piers Morgan, and Sharon Osbourne, which he said added legitimacy to his career.

cards.headline: Florida budget signing expected Monday ahead of new fiscal year
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis is expected to sign the state budget Monday, just ahead of the new fiscal year beginning July 1, with more vetoes anticipated specifically targeting line items in the spending plan.
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis vetoed two bills Friday night. He rejected HB 325, which would have extended commercial driver's license training to nonviolent inmates with two years or less remaining on their sentences. The bill passed unanimously in both chambers, but DeSantis said lawmakers overlooked unintended consequences, calling the program unnecessarily burdensome to the Department of Corrections and expressing concern that training inmates to drive creates significant public safety concerns. He also vetoed SB 688, which would have created a Board of Naturopathic Medicine within the Department of Health to set guidelines for practitioners.

DeSantis has also previously vetoed a bill to track e-bike and scooter crashes and a measure making it easier for high school students to volunteer as poll workers. More vetoes are expected as line items in the budget, which DeSantis is scheduled to sign Monday, ahead of the new fiscal year beginning July 1.

cards.headline: 78-year-old woman dies after SUV rolls backward in Port St. Lucie driveway
cards.teaser: A woman was killed Sunday morning when an SUV rolled backward and struck her at a residence on SE El Sito Court.
cards.body: A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The incident happened at approximately 10:47 a.m. when the woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door. The SUV began rolling backward, and the open door struck her, knocking her to the ground. Her 59-year-old son was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The woman was rushed to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation.
